newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-QUESADA STAYS COOL TO TAKE WORLD TRIPLE JUMP TITLE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-QUESADA STAYS COOL TO TAKE WORLD TRIPLE JUMP TITLE.

text.p: If there were gold medals given for staying cool under pressure, world triple jump champion Yoelvis Quesada could stake a claim.
Despite having the reigning world champion and world record holder breathing down his neck, the Cuban maintained that he had hardly broken sweat during Friday's competition.
"I was never worried at all, especially after my 17.85 jump in the second round," Quesada said.
The leap was the best in the world this year, a Cuban national record and sufficient for the gold medal.
"I always thought it would be good enough to win," Quesada added.
The Cuban took the lead with his first round jump of 17.60 then another effort of 17.60 in the third round was followed a round later by a foul before Quesada decided to pass his final two attempts.

Briton Jonathan Edwards, who set current world record of 18.29 while winning the 1995 title, tried to close the gap and moved into the silver medal position with his fourth round 17.66 before improving to 17.69 with his final effort.
"I know Edwards and have competed against him many times. I wasn't worried by him although I respect him and watched him," Quesada commented.
Edwards and the American Olympic champion Kenny Harrison are both over 30 while Quesada celebrated his 24th birthday on Monday.

"You only need to look at the way Edwards jumped to know that he is not finished," Quesada said. "I don't think Harrison is either. However in a certain moment I might be able to attack the 18 metre mark."
Quesada became the third Cuban jumper to strike gold at these world championships following earlier successes by long jumper Ivan Pedroso and high jumper Javier Sotomayor.
"In Cuba we have a good tradition of jumpers. All the kids want to jump,"said Quesada. "Good jumpers are like water in Cuba, plentiful."
Edwards was bitterly disappointed at losing his world title.
"I didn't really have my normal rhythm. I'm just a bit numb at the moment. However I feel I've still got the potential to jump over 18 metres - maybe even over 18.29," Edwards said.
Quesada's compatriot Aliecer Urrutia, the 1997 world indoor silver medallist, took third place with 17.64.
